title: Mastering Keratoconus: The Amsler-Krumeich Framework & Beyond
summary: Keratoconus (KC) is a progressive, non-inflammatory ectatic disorder characterized by corneal thinning and protrusion. This infographic details the clinical staging, diagnostic markers, and evidence-based management of KC, focusing on the gold-standard Amsler-Krumeich classification.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Keratoconus is a bilateral, typically asymmetric corneal ectasia. It involves progressive stromal thinning, Bowman’s layer fragmentation, and iron deposition in the basal epithelium (Fleischer ring), leading to irregular astigmatism, high myopia, and decreased best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA).

branches: Genetic: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21), Leber Congenital Amaurosis
Connective Tissue: Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan Syndrome, Osteogenesis Imperfecta
Environmental: Chronic UV exposure, Atopic dermatitis
Biochemical: Increased Lysosomal enzymes, decreased Protease inhibitors

sections.title: Clinical Signs: Slit-Lamp Findings
content: Fleischer Ring: Iron deposition at the base of the cone (best with cobalt blue filter).
Vogt Striae: Fine, vertical stress lines in deep stroma/Descemet membrane (disappear with digital pressure).
Munson Sign: V-shaped indentation of the lower lid on down-gaze.
Rizzuti Sign: Conical reflection on the nasal iris when light is shone from the temporal side.
Charleux Sign: Oil-droplet reflex on distant ophthalmoscopy.
Prominent Corneal Nerves: Visible in the stroma.

content.explanation: Vogt striae, Fleischer ring, Munson sign, Rizzuti sign.

rows: Crescent-shaped thinning 1-2mm from inferior limbus; 'Butterfly' pattern on topography.
Generalized, globular thinning from limbus to limbus; maximal peripherally.
Increased curvature of the posterior corneal surface only; usually non-progressive.
Superior thinning with lipid deposits and vascularization; usually older patients.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: 1. Corneal Topography: Placcido-based mapping of the anterior surface.
2. Corneal Tomography (Pentacam/Galilei): Elevation mapping of BOTH anterior and posterior surfaces.
3. Pachymetry: Measuring the thinnest point (crucial for CXL candidacy).
4. Epithelial Mapping (OCT): Characteristic epithelial thinning over the cone apex.
5. Biomechanics (Corvis ST/ORA): Measuring Corneal Hysteresis (CH) and Resistance Factor (CRF).

sections.title: Red Flags: Acute Hydrops
content: Sudden, painful vision loss.
Severe corneal edema (Descemet membrane rupture).
Intrastromal clefts on OCT.
Risk of perforation (rare but critical).
Management: Topical hypertonics, cycloplegics, and observation (Avoid emergency PKP).

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: Step 1 (Early): Spectacles or Soft Toric Contact Lenses.
Step 2 (Moderate): Rigid Gas Permeable (RGP) or Scleral Lenses for irregular astigmatism.
Step 3 (Progression): Corneal Collagen Cross-linking (CXL) to stabilize the cornea (Dresden Protocol).
Step 4 (Alternative): Intrastromal Corneal Ring Segments (ICRS) to flatten the cone and improve lens fit.
Step 5 (Late/Scarred): Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty (DALK) - Preferred if endothelium is healthy.
Step 6 (End-stage): Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP) if full-thickness scarring or previous hydrops exists.

sections.title: Corneal Cross-linking (CXL) Protocol
content: Standard (Dresden): 30 mins Riboflavin (0.1%) soaking + 30 mins UVA (3 mW/cm²).
Epi-Off: Gold standard; requires removal of central 8-9mm of epithelium.
Epi-On: Lower risk of infection/haze but potentially less effective.
Accelerated CXL: Higher intensity UVA for shorter duration (e.g., 9-30 mW/cm²).
Inclusion: Progressive KC with pachymetry > 400 µm (or 320 µm with hypotonic riboflavin).

sections.title: Contraindications for CXL
content: Corneal thickness < 400 µm (standard protocol).
Prior Herpes Simplex Keratitis (risk of reactivation).
Severe central corneal scarring.
Active ocular infection or severe ocular surface disease.
Pregnancy (hormonal changes affect ectasia).

rows: Radius of curvature in the thinnest 3mm zone (anterior).
Radius of curvature in the thinnest 3mm zone (posterior).

sections.title: Surgical Pearls
content: ICRS: Place at 70-80% depth; goal is 'arc-shortening' effect.
DALK: Big Bubble technique (Dua/Anwar) allows for bare Descemet exposure.
PKP in KC: Excellent prognosis (>90% graft survival at 10 years).
Post-Op: Watch for 'Urrets-Zavalia Syndrome' (permanent iris atrophy/mydriasis) after keratoplasty.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always screen family members of KC patients.
Stop contact lens wear (RGP 2 weeks, Soft 1 week) before topography.
Atopy must be controlled to prevent eye rubbing and progression.
Progressive KC in children is more aggressive; consider early CXL.
